court: County Court of New York, Cayuga County
notes: Liquor-tax consent proceeding turning on whether a subdivided rear structure counts as separate 'dwellings'; passing mention that some occupants boarded is incidental, not about the legal character of letting rooms or regulation of lodging.

Local-option election resubmission dispute (town-meeting notice defects, Soldiers' Home residency); mentions hotel liquor sales to transient guests only as background for the petitioners' hardship argument, not lodging law.

holding_summary: A hotel keeper with thirty-two furnished rooms for lodgers, a restaurant and a bar sought to enjoin police from posting officers and inspecting his premises and from telling prospective customers it was a disorderly house. The court held the police captain had statutory authority to inspect and post officers at a licensed liquor premises, but enjoined the officers from telling customers the place was disorderly and liable to be raided, since suppressing a nuisance out of court in that manner was unlawful oppression.

quotes.text: that said premises contain thirty-two furnished-rooms for lodgers, a restaurant and a bar;

There seems, therefore, to be abundant authority in the statutes and the cases for the captain of police taking such action as his discretion warrants for posting his officers and making his inspections.
So far, then, as he and his officers interfered with the customers of this place by statements as to its character and threats of possible raids, he proceeds, in my judgment, without warrant of law.

notes: Police-power inspection of a licensed lodging hotel sustained; informal out-of-court branding of the business as a disorderly house enjoined. Mixed: regulation upheld in part, commercial letting business protected in part.
Bank-building column encroachment onto a public sidewalk; 'incident of ownership' language concerns vaults/cellarways under sidewalks, not letting rooms or dwellings. False-positive retrieval.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: Pleading dispute over whether a counterclaim in a saloon-lease dispossess proceeding was properly a set-off; a liquor-license side issue, not about letting rooms/dwellings or lodging regulation.
Restrictive-covenant/riparian-rights dispute over a vaudeville theatre and drinking-place structure built below high-water mark; unrelated to letting rooms or dwellings for lodging.
Ordinary year-term whole-house lease surrender dispute (keys, linoleum, 'To Let' sign); not a lodging/boarding arrangement or short-term room letting.

holding_summary: Land was subject to a covenant restricting use to private residences and barring business, saloon, and restaurant uses. The defendant had long operated her premises as a private hotel/boarding-house for permanent summer guests who lodged and took meals there, which the court (following Murray v. Charman) held did not violate the covenant since furnishing food and liquor to such guests was merely incidental to the lodging business. However, converting one building into a separate, publicly-open restaurant and drinking saloon not limited to house guests was a clear violation and was enjoined.

quotes.text: the defendant had used the premises owned by her for a private hotel or boarding-house for the entertainment of gentlemen and their families, who desired to spend the heated term in the country.

the maintenance of a private hotel or boarding-house, in which the furnishing of food and liquor to its guests, to be served with their meals or in their private rooms, was only incidental to the principal business there carried on, was not a violation of the covenants in question.

notes: Directly on point: court treats operating a private hotel/boarding-house for paying guests as compatible with a residential-only restrictive covenant, distinguishing it from a standalone public restaurant/saloon use, which was enjoined as a true business intrusion.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: Real-estate broker's commission dispute over securing a lease tenant; no facts about the premises' residential/lodging character or type of occupancy.
Restrictive covenant limiting Madison Avenue lots to private residences, defendant sought to convert to stores/offices; a business-use covenant case, not lodging/boarding.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: Res judicata dispute over whether a prior default judgment established a month-to-month tenancy for dispossess purposes; ordinary apartment tenancy, no lodging/boarding-house facts.

holding_summary: Plaintiff, described as a boarding-house keeper, sued for treble damages after defendant forcibly entered and tore down part of her residence/kitchen, disrupting her boarding-house business. The court denied treble damages only because the complaint failed to plead a claim under the forcible-entry-and-detainer statute, not because the boarding-house business itself was unlawful or unprotected.

quotes.text: the plaintiff’s business, that of a boarding-house keeper, was injured, and her property was broken and destroyed, and her health injured

notes: Thin but on-point: boarding-house keeping is treated by the court as an ordinary lawful business whose disruption is compensable; the only defect was pleading treble damages under the wrong theory, not the legality of the boarding-house business.
Landlord's assignee's right to treat a holding-over commercial tenant as a tenant for another year; no lodging/boarding facts.
Liquor-tax certificate revocation over sufficiency of neighboring-dwelling-owner consents and building entrances; consent-counting mechanics, not lodging/boarding regulation or letting.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: Street-railway collision personal-injury case; no relation to letting dwellings or lodging regulation. Retrieval mismatch.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: Eviction/constructive-eviction dispute between a landlord and the commercial lessee running the Albemarle Hotel, arising from adjoining construction damage. Concerns the landlord-tenant lease of the hotel business itself, not the legal character of guests' compensated occupancy or regulation of lodging.
Building setback-line restrictive covenant dispute over a two-family house; no lodging/boarding facts.
Ejectment/adverse-possession dispute among cotenant heirs over title to real property; no lodging/boarding or short-term letting facts.
